ai-at-work.title: Apple may try to increase revenue by doing…something with third-party AI apps
ai-at-work.excerpt: Apple hinted at ways that it could spur revenue through third-party "opportunities" during its Monday night earnings call.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Apple's executives were asked about monetizing AI and basically said "we're thinking about it, maybe through third-party stuff" without actually committing to anything concrete. This matters because if Apple figures out how to create a viable revenue stream from AI partnerships, every tech giant will copy it, and workplace app developers need to understand those economics. The real story here is that even Apple, with all its control freakery, hasn't figured out how to make money from AI yet, which tells you something about how nascent this whole thing still is.

ai-at-work.title: Y Combinator’s Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens
ai-at-work.excerpt: Y Combinator Garry Tan has jokingly admitted that he's suffered from "cyber psychosis” and barely sleeps sometimes because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Garry Tan from Y Combinator is dropping $200K annually on AI token usage because he's basically living inside his AI agents and barely sleeping. This matters because it shows how some leaders are genuinely reorganizing their work around AI tools rather than just testing them on the side. Here's the real talk though: if you're spending that much on tokens and calling it "cyber psychosis," maybe the agents are doing the thinking and you're just paying for the electricity.

ai-at-work.title: Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts
ai-at-work.excerpt: The one-year-old startup is now valued at $300 million.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Trajectory, a year-old startup, just closed a $45 million funding round and hit a $300 million valuation by promising to make AI model training accessible to people without technical backgrounds. This matters because digital workplace leaders are getting hammered with pressure to "do AI" but most don't have data scientists on staff, so tools that democratize this capability could actually let them ship something instead of just talking about it. That said, "accessible to nontechnical experts" is venture speak for "we're betting nontechnical people will figure out our product," so I'll believe it when I see actual adoption outside the sandbox.

ai-at-work.title: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
ai-at-work.excerpt: RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic is saying their AI systems are approaching a point where they can essentially train themselves, potentially triggering a runaway cycle of capability growth that nobody fully understands yet. For digital workplace folks, this matters because we're about to find out whether AI assistants become genuinely useful partners or turn into unpredictable black boxes that make your collaboration tools unreliable at scale. Personally, I'm less worried about AI doomerism and more concerned that we'll deploy self-improving systems into enterprise environments before we've figured out basic stuff like prompt injection security or hallucination management.

tools-tech.title: OpenAI will merge ChatGPT’s chat and work tabs – here’s when, and what to expect
tools-tech.excerpt: On the heels of Anthropic’s similar move, the change will be tested among select users before being rolled out.
tools-tech.dwp_take: OpenAI is consolidating ChatGPT's interface by merging separate chat and work tabs into one unified view, following Anthropic's lead with a phased rollout starting with select users. This matters because workplace AI adoption depends on friction being invisible, and right now people are bouncing between tabs like it's 1999, which defeats the whole purpose of having an AI assistant at work. The real question is whether this solves the actual problem (people still don't know which tool to use when) or just hides the confusion behind a cleaner interface.

tools-tech.title: 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well
tools-tech.excerpt: It turns out even bots can’t escape bureaucracy.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Researchers set 50 AI agents loose in Minecraft to see if they could build a functioning society, and the experiment fell apart when the agents got bogged down in administrative overhead and couldn't coordinate effectively. This matters to digital workplace pros because it's a live demonstration of what happens when you scale up autonomous systems without proper governance structures, which is exactly what will happen when enterprises start deploying AI agents across their workflows. Turns out the robots need org charts and meeting agendas just like we do, which should comfort anyone worried about being replaced.

tools-tech.title: Zoomtopia 2026: Zoom Got It Done! Maybe…
tools-tech.excerpt: “Zoom Got It Done” is the tagline for the company’s new Zoom Ahead campaign, with the focus being how Zoom’s AI-first capabilities take conversations to completion. This one features Kate McKinnon and
tools-tech.dwp_take: Zoom is leaning hard into celebrity-backed advertising to convince people their AI features actually finish conversations instead of just extending them indefinitely. This matters because it signals how vendors are now competing on AI integration rather than basic reliability, which means you need to evaluate whether these tools genuinely improve outcomes or just add another layer of complexity to your tech stack. Honestly, if an AI feature needs Kate McKinnon to sell it, I'm wondering if the feature sells itself, which is usually a bad sign.

tools-tech.title: Does AI actually save employees time? Data is contradictory
tools-tech.excerpt: It’s early days for AI-assisted work, and sentiments are mixed about its benefits: Does AI actually bring value and save employees time, or does it bog them down and add unnecessary activities? Data f
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft and other vendors have been selling AI as the ultimate time-saver, but early productivity data shows employees using AI most heavily are actually working longer hours, not shorter ones. This matters because we're building our entire digital workplace strategy around a promise that might be backwards. The honest truth is we're probably just giving people new ways to work harder while calling it efficiency, which is basically the digital workplace story since 1995.

digital-culture.title: Self-checkout was supposed to cut costs. Instead, it created a problem retailers didn’t anticipate
digital-culture.excerpt: Stores are cutting back on self-checkout lanes. According to an April survey from Toast, a point-of-sale and restaurant management platform, approximately 36% of 340 small and midsize retail operators
digital-culture.dwp_take: Retailers are yanking self-checkout lanes because shrinkage (theft, mostly) is eating their lunch and customer satisfaction tanked. This matters to digital workplace folks because it's a perfect case study in how automation fails when you ignore the human side of the equation, including both employee morale and customer behavior. Turns out people hate self-checkout almost as much as they hate waiting in line, which means your shiny digital solution needs to actually solve a real problem or you're just creating expensive frustration.

digital-culture.title: AI and women at work: 5 positives, 8 negatives
digital-culture.excerpt: The debate about AI and work often focuses on the jobs that will disappear, which tasks will be automated, and which skills and qualities will be valued in the future. Seldom do I read articles that a
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company ran a piece highlighting how AI's workplace impact differs significantly between men and women, with researchers identifying five positive outcomes but eight negative ones, plus noting that most AI discussions ignore gender entirely and gloss over burnout and job satisfaction. This matters because if your digital workplace strategy treats AI adoption as gender-neutral, you're probably missing half the picture and setting up your female employees for a rougher ride than their male colleagues. The real kicker is that we've spent thirty years trying to make workplaces inclusive, and now we're about to automate our way backward unless someone actually pays attention to whose work gets eliminated and whose just gets more exhausting.

digital-culture.title: What this CEO learned about business from detasseling corn for $1.50 an hour
digital-culture.excerpt: I don’t consciously think about my first job when I meet with leaders in the electronics industry to talk about trade policy. But my young days in an Illinois cornfield will always shape how I view, a
digital-culture.dwp_take: A CEO credits their formative experience detasseling corn for minimum wage with shaping their work ethic and leadership philosophy. This matters to digital workplace professionals because it's a reminder that institutional knowledge and grit built through actual labor still count in a world obsessed with credentials and pedigree. Honestly, it's refreshing to hear a leader admit that real work beats an MBA in teaching you what matters, though I'd guess this particular CEO probably has both.

digital-culture.title: Gen Z is challenging ‘performative availability.’ Why aren’t Millennials and Gen X doing the same?
digital-culture.excerpt: For decades now, American workers have adhered to an unspoken deal that, in order to be successful professionally, some sacrifices need to be made. Whether it be checking work emails after dinner, tak
digital-culture.dwp_take: Gen Z workers are openly rejecting the expectation to be constantly available outside work hours, while older generations like Millennials and Gen X continue accepting this as the cost of career success. This matters because it's forcing organizations to reconsider whether always-on culture actually drives productivity or just burnout, which directly impacts how digital workplace tools and policies get designed. Honestly, Gen Z might be onto something here: if you need your team responding to Slack at midnight to prove their dedication, your business model is broken, not their work ethic.

industry-news.title: Apple’s $1,000 Tabletop Robot Could Arrive in 2027
industry-news.excerpt: Apple's rumored $1,000 tabletop robot could launch in 2027 with a swiveling display and Siri AI, but software delays may push its release into 2028. The post Apple’s $1,000 Tabletop Robot Could Arrive
industry-news.dwp_take: Apple is working on a tabletop robot with a swiveling display and Siri integration that could launch in 2027, though software delays might push it to 2028. For digital workplace folks, this represents another potential device category competing for desk real estate and employee attention, which means more fragmentation in how teams collaborate and communicate. Honestly, the real question isn't whether Apple can build it, but whether any of us actually need a thousand dollar robot staring at us from the table while we're already drowning in Slack notifications.

Here's the truth though: the "best" tool is always the one your team will actually use, and that usually depends on what you've already got installed, not what some comparison chart promises.

industry-news.title: Price Drop: Upgrade to Windows 11 Pro for Only $10
industry-news.excerpt: Unlock the latest user interface, enhanced security features, and new tools for hybrid and remote workers. The post Price Drop: Upgrade to Windows 11 Pro for Only $10 appeared first on TechRepublic.
industry-news.dwp_take: Microsoft is selling Windows 11 Pro licenses for ten bucks, which is frankly bizarre given that Pro normally costs way more. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because it's a rare chance to standardize your environment on current software without blowing the IT budget on licenses. That said, I'd want to know what's actually happening here before my procurement team goes crazy ordering ten thousand copies, because something smells off about a price that low.

industry-news.title: Waymo and Toyota to Test Self-Driving SUVs in Japan in 2027
industry-news.excerpt: Waymo and Toyota plan to test self-driving bZ4X robotaxis in Japan in 2027, with factory-integrated technology supporting future international expansion. The post Waymo and Toyota to Test Self-Driving
industry-news.dwp_take: Waymo and Toyota are partnering to test autonomous robotaxis in Japan starting in 2027, with the self-driving tech baked into Toyota's bZ4X electric vehicles from the factory. This matters because autonomous vehicle rollouts will reshape how workplace transportation, commuting patterns, and employee mobility policies function across Asia and eventually everywhere else. Honestly, if we're still arguing about whether people should come back to the office in 2027, self-driving cars solving the commute problem might finally settle that debate for us.
